source_text: Ἔξεστι δὲ ἡμῖν ἐκ περιουσίας πρὸς τοὺς φιλεγκλήμονας ἐπαποδύσασθαι· οὐ γὰρ παῖδες ἡμεῖς καὶ νήπιοι πρὸς τὸ παιδαριῶδες καὶ εὐκαταφρόνητον τῆς μαθήσεως προσηγορεύμεθα, καθὼς οἱ εἰς γνῶσιν πεφυσιωμένοι διαβεβλήκασιν· ἀναγεννηθέντες γοῦν εὐθέως τὸ τέλειον ἀπειλήφαμεν, οὗ ἕνεκεν ἐσπεύδομεν. ἐφωτίσθημεν γάρ· τὸ δὲ ἔστιν ἐπιγνῶναι τὸν θεόν. οὔκουν ἀτελὴς ὁ ἐγνωκὼς τὸ τέλειον. καί μου μὴ λάβησθε ὁμολογοῦντος ἐγνωκέναι τὸν θεόν. ὧδέ πως γὰρ ἔδοξεν εἰπεῖν τῷ λόγῳ· ὃ δὲ ἐλεύθερος. αὐτίκα γοῦν βαπτιζομένῳ τῷ κυρίῳ ἀπ᾿ οὐρανῶν ἐπήχησε φωνὴ μάρτυς ἠγαπημένου »υἱός μου εἶ σὺ ἀγαπητός, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε.« πυθώμεθα οὖν τῶν σοφῶν· σήμερον ἀναγεννηθεὶς ὁ Χριστὸς ἤδη τέλειός ἐστιν ἤ, ὅπερ ἀτοπώτατον, ἐλλιπής. εἰ δὲ τοῦτο, προσμαθεῖν τι αὐτῷ δεῖ. ἀλλὰ προσμαθεῖν μὲν αὐτὸν εἰκὸς οὐδὲ ἓν θεὸν ὄντα. οὐ γὰρ ἂν μείζων τις εἴη τοῦ λόγου οὐδὲ μὴν διδάσκαλος τοῦ μόνου διδασκάλου. μή τι οὖν ὁμολογήσουσιν ἄκοντες τὸν λόγον, τέλειον ἐκ τελείου φύντα τοῦ πατρός, κατὰ τὴν οἰκονομικὴν προδιατύπωσιν ἀναγεννηθῆναι τελείως; καὶ εἰ τέλειος ἦν, τί ἐβαπτίζετο ὁ τέλειος; ἔδει, φασί, πληρῶσαι τὸ ἐπάγγελμα τὸ ἀνθρώπινον. παγκάλως. φημὶ γάρ· ἅμα τοίνυν τῷ βαπτίζεσθαι αὐτὸν ὑπὸ Ἰωάννου γίνεται τέλειος; δῆλον ὅτι. οὐδὲν οὖν πρὸς αὐτοῦ προσέμαθεν; οὐ γάρ. τελειοῦται δὲ τῷ λουτρῷ μόνῳ καὶ τοῦ πνεύματος τῇ καθόδῳ ἁγιάζεται; οὕτως ἔχει. Τὸ δὲ αὐτὸ συμβαίνει τοῦτο καὶ περὶ ἡμᾶς, ὧν γέγονεν ὑπογραφὴ ὁ κύριος· βαπτιζόμενοι φωτιζόμεθα, φωτιζόμενοι υἱοποιούμεθα, υἱοποιούμενοι τελειούμεθα, τελειούμενοι ἀπαθανατιζόμεθα »ἐγώ«, φησίν, »εἶπα, θεοί ἐστε καὶ υἱοὶ ὑψίστου πάντες.« καλεῖται δὲ πολλαχῶς τὸ ἔργον τοῦτο, χάρισμα καὶ φώτισμα καὶ τέλειον καὶ λουτρόν· λουτρὸν μὲν δι᾿ οὗ τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἀπορρυπτόμεθα, χάρισμα δὲ ᾧ τὰ ἐπὶ τοῖς ἁμαρτήμασιν ἐπιτίμια ἀνεῖται, φώτισμα δὲ δι᾿ οὗ τὸ ἅγιον ἐκεῖνο φῶς τὸ σωτήριον ἐποπτεύεται, τουτέστιν δι᾿ οὗ τὸ θεῖον ὀξυωποῦμεν, τέλειον δὲ τὸ ἀπροσδεὲς φαμέν. τί γὰρ ἔτι λείπεται τῷ θεὸν ἐγνωκότι; καὶ γὰρ ἄτοπον ὡς ἀληθῶς χάρισμα κεκλῆσθαι θεοῦ τὸ μὴ πεπληρωμένον· τέλειος δὲ ὢν τέλεια χαριεῖται δήπουθεν· ὡς δὲ ἅμα τῷ κελεῦσαι αὐτὸν πάντα γίνεται, οὕτως ἕπεται τῷ χαρίσασθαι μόνον βουληθῆναι αὐτὸν τὸ πεπληρῶσθαι τὴν χάριν. τὸ γὰρ μέλλον τοῦ χρόνου τῇ δυνάμει τοῦ θελήματος προλαμβάνεται. πρὸς δὲ καὶ ἡ τῶν κακῶν ἀπαλλαγὴ σωτηρίας ἐστὶν ἀρχή. μόνον δὲ ἄρα οἱ πρῶτον δραξάμενοι τῶν ὅρων τῆς ζωῆς ἤδη τέλειοι, ζῶμεν δὲ ἤδη οἱ θανάτου κεχωρισμένοι. σωτηρία τοίνυν τὸ ἕπεσθαι Χριστῷ. »ὃ γὰρ γέγονεν ἐν αὐτῷ, ζωή ἐστιν.« »ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν,« φησίν, »ὁ τὸν λόγον μου ἀκούων καὶ πιστεύων τῷ πέμψαντί με ἔχει ζωὴν αἰώνιον καὶ εἰς κρίσιν οὐκ ἔρχεται, ἀλλὰ μεταβέβηκεν ἐκ τοῦ θανάτου εἰς τὴν ζωήν.« οὕτω τὸ πιστεῦσαι μόνον καὶ ἀναγεννηθῆναι τελείωσίς ἐστιν ἐν ζωῇ· οὐ γάρ ποτε ἀσθενεῖ ὁ θεός.
pass_a_gloss: It is possible for us from abundance to put off for those who love to be destitute; for we are not children and infants to be called towards the childish and easily despised thing of learning, as those who have been brought to knowledge have slandered; for having been reborn we immediately received the perfect thing, on account of which we hurry. For we have been enlightened; and this is to know God. Therefore the one who has known the perfect thing is not imperfect. And do not take hold of me as confessing to have known God. For thus somehow it seemed right to the Word to speak; which is free. For immediately to the Lord being baptized from heaven a voice sounded as a witness of the beloved: 'You are my son, my beloved, today I have begotten you.' Let us then learn from the wise; today having been reborn, is Christ already perfect or, which is most absurd, imperfect? But if this, it is necessary for him to learn something. But it is fitting for him to learn nothing, being God. For no one would be greater than the Word, nor even a teacher of the only Teacher. Will they not then unwillingly confess the Word, perfect from the perfect Father, to have been reborn perfectly according to the economic pre-arrangement? And if he was perfect, why was the perfect one baptized? It was necessary, they say, to fulfill the human promise. Beautifully, I say; for does he become perfect at the same time as being baptized by John? Clearly. Did he then learn nothing in addition to this? No. Is he then perfected by the bath alone and sanctified by the descent of the Spirit? It holds thus. The same thing happens also concerning us, of whom the Lord has become a guarantee; being baptized we are enlightened, being enlightened we are made sons, being made sons we are perfected, being perfected we are made immortal. 'I', he says, 'said, you are gods and all sons of the Most High.' And this work is called by many names, a gift and enlightenment and perfect and bath; a bath, indeed, through which we wash away sins, a gift by which the penalties for sins are forgiven, enlightenment through which that holy and saving light is beheld, that is, through which we perceive the divine, perfect we say is that which is not in need of anything. For what is still lacking to the one who has known God? And it is also absurd, truly, for the gift of God to be called imperfect; but being perfect, he will surely give perfect gifts; just as all things come into being at the same time as his command, so also it follows that to his giving only his will is required for the gift to be fulfilled. For the future is anticipated by the power of his will. And besides, the removal of evils is the beginning of salvation. Only then, those who have first grasped the boundaries of life are already perfect, and we who have been separated from death are already living. Salvation, then, is to follow Christ. 'For what has come into being in him is life.' 'Amen, amen, I say to you', he says, 'the one who hears my word and believes in the one who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life.' Thus to believe alone and to be reborn is perfection in life; for God is never weak.

pass_b_english: We have the freedom to let go of our abundance and give to those in need, for we are not immature or childish in our approach to learning, as some might claim. Having been reborn, we immediately receive the perfect gift, and this is what drives us forward. Our enlightenment is, in fact, our knowledge of God. The person who has experienced this perfect gift is not incomplete. I'm not claiming to have fully known God, but rather, I'm speaking from the perspective of the Word, which is free. When the Lord was baptized, a voice from heaven testified, saying, 'You are my beloved Son, today I have begotten you' (Matthew 3:17). So, let's consider the wisdom of this event: is the reborn Christ already perfect, or is he somehow imperfect? If he's imperfect, then he must still have something to learn. But if he's God, it's only fitting that he has nothing to learn, for no one is greater than the Word, and no one can teach the one who is the only Teacher. Won't they reluctantly admit that the Word, who is perfect and comes from the perfect Father, was reborn in a perfect way, according to God's plan? And if Christ was already perfect, why did he need to be baptized? Some say it was necessary to fulfill human obligations. I say, beautifully, that Christ's baptism was a moment of perfection, and it's clear that he didn't learn anything new in that moment. He was perfected through his baptism and sanctified by the descent of the Spirit. This same process applies to us, who have the Lord as our guarantee. Through baptism, we are enlightened; through enlightenment, we become children of God; through becoming children of God, we are perfected; and through perfection, we become immortal. As it's written, 'You are gods, and all of you are children of the Most High' (John 1:12-13). This transformative work is known by many names: a gift, enlightenment, perfection, and baptism. Baptism is the washing away of sins; a gift is the forgiveness of penalties for sins; enlightenment is the experience of the holy and saving light, which allows us to perceive the divine. We call it perfect because it lacks nothing. What could possibly be lacking for someone who has known God? It's absurd to think that God's gift could be imperfect; instead, the perfect God gives perfect gifts. Just as all things come into being at the moment of God's command, so too does the fulfillment of God's gift require only God's will. The future is anticipated by the power of God's will, and the removal of evil is the beginning of salvation. Only those who have grasped the boundaries of life are already perfect, and we who have been separated from death are already living. Salvation, then, is a matter of following Christ, for 'what has come into being in him is life' (John 5:24). As Jesus says, 'The one who hears my word and believes in the one who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life.' To believe and be reborn is to experience perfection in life, for God is never weak.

review.notes: Pass B fails on agency and accuracy regarding the Greek text. In the clause 'ἐκ περιουσίας πρὸς τοὺς φιλεγκλήμονας ἐπαποδύσασθαι', Pass A translates 'from abundance to put off for those who love to be destitute', which is a semantic error (it means to give away from one's own possessions to those who love misery/poverty). Pass B attempts to fix this but changes the meaning to 'freedom to let go of our abundance and give to those in need', which introduces an agency/modality shift not present in the Greek. More critically, Pass B misidentifies the scripture citation for 'εἶπα, θεοί ἐστε καὶ υἱοὶ ὑψίστου πάντες' (I said, you are gods and all sons of the Most High). Pass B cites 'John 1:12-13', but the Greek text is a direct quotation of Psalm 82:6 (as cited in Matthew 5:48 or similar contexts), and the wording 'you are gods' is not found in John 1:12-13. Furthermore, Pass B's translation of 'οὐ γὰρ ἂν μείζων τις εἴη τοῦ λόγου' as 'no one can teach the one who is the only Teacher' is a significant departure from the Greek 'nor even a teacher of the only Teacher'.
reasons: Pass B provides a false scripture citation for 'εἶπα, θεοί ἐστε καὶ υἱοὶ ὑψίστου πάντες' (Psalm 82:6) by labeling it 'John 1:12-13'.

Pass B misrepresents the Greek 'οὐ γὰρ ἂν μείζων τις εἴη τοῦ λόγου οὐδὲ μὴν διδάσκαλος τοῦ μόνου διδασκάλου' by translating it as 'no one can teach the one who is the only Teacher', losing the comparative 'nor even a teacher of the only Teacher'.
